bull_thesis: Yelp is a genuinely high-quality business trading at a distressed-cheap price because the market has decided artificial-intelligence search will kill local-review sites. Three things make this more than optical cheapness. First, the durable half of the business is bigger than the market credits: Services advertising (plumbers, contractors, auto and home pros) is $948M of the $1.46B top line, still the majority, and it is the half consumers use with real purchase intent — a lead-generation and job-completion job that a pure chat answer does not yet complete. Second, the buyback is a powerful, self-funding value engine: management has retired about 22% of the fully diluted share count over four years (86M to 67M shares) and roughly 11% in just the last two quarters, so at a ~20% free-cash-flow yield each repurchased dollar compounds per-share value even if revenue never grows. Third, artificial intelligence is being monetized, not just feared: 'other revenue' grew 75% year-over-year in the first quarter of 2026, Yelp has signed a data-licensing agreement with OpenAI and its content now appears on Apple Maps, Amazon Alexa, Microsoft Bing and Meta.ai, the Hatch acquisition is growing ~92%, and management targets a $250M annual run-rate in these lines by the end of 2028 (more than double today). bear_thesis: The bear case is that this is a cheap-looking asset that is slowly melting, and the cheapness is the market pricing that correctly. The engagement base that feeds the entire model is shrinking: ad clicks fell 7%, 11% and 10% year-over-year in the last three quarters, app unique devices are down 2%, and paying advertising locations have dropped from 517,000 to 485,000 (down 6% year-over-year) — the customer count is now falling across both segments, not just Restaurants, Retail & Other. Revenue growth has decelerated to 1%, and the supposed growth engine, Services advertising, slowed from 14% to roughly 1% in five quarters. Earnings are actually going backwards in 2026: net income fell 27% year-over-year in the first quarter, net margin halved from 10% to 5%, adjusted operating profit fell 7%, and the live analyst consensus models earnings per share declining to about $1.88 this year from $2.24 — the opposite of the screener's stale '+39% forward growth' figure. The structural threat is real and worsening: generative-AI search (ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity) lets consumers get a local recommendation without ever visiting Yelp, which would collapse the ad impressions that are roughly 90% of revenue. The larger one, advertising to home and professional services - plumbers, electricians, contractors, auto repair - runs at about $948 million a year and grew 1% in the first quarter of 2026. The smaller advertising business - restaurants, retail and other - runs at about $404 million and fell 11% in the first quarter of 2026. That one is genuinely melting. The bull case does not deny it; it says you are already being compensated for it several times over.

Then there is the part nobody is paying for. Other revenue reached $29 million in the first quarter of 2026, up 75% year over year, and roughly $32 million in the second quarter. It has three legs, all growing fast and all higher-margin than advertising. Data licensing: Yelp has signed Amazon Alexa, Apple Maps, Microsoft Bing, Meta.ai, Yahoo and, in February 2026, OpenAI, to license its 330 million reviews, 500 million photos and 8 million business listings - the exact asset every conversational assistant needs and cannot cheaply build. Software: Hatch, acquired in February 2026, was at a $34 million annual run rate in March growing 92%; Yelp Host passed one million calls answered by June 2026, having grown at an average 38% a month since its October 2025 launch, and management sizes its United States market at over $1 billion. Transactions: food ordering revenue grew 88% year over year on the DoorDash partnership. Management targets a $250 million annual run rate for this combined line by the end of 2028, more than double the current pace. On 2026-09-10 Yelp and Hatch became among the first deployers of OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 voice model - the company that is supposed to kill Yelp is instead its supplier and its customer.

The quality of the business supports the case. Gross margin is 88.9%. Return on invested capital is about 9% and return on equity 12.4% - modest in absolute terms, but set against Tripadvisor's 1.2% return on invested capital and Angi's negative 17%, Yelp is the only member of its peer group actually earning money. Management has beaten the top end of its own revenue guidance in all seven of the last seven quarters, and beaten its adjusted profit guidance by $11 million to $15 million a quarter. And the share count has fallen hard: fully diluted shares went from 86 million at the end of 2021 to 67 million at the end of 2025, and the weighted diluted count was 55.7 million in the second quarter of 2026 - down another 10% in just two quarters. Every dollar of flat earnings is spread across a steadily smaller base.

Finally, positioning. Seven brokers cover the stock, the consensus recommendation was Reduce as of 2026-08-31, there has been no rating change by anyone since 2026-05-15, and not a single price target was published in the last quarter - the most recent is 130 days old. The stock is at its 52-week low, 24% below its 200-day average. There is essentially nobody left to sell it on the next disappointment.

Conditions this case depends on: services advertising must hold near flat rather than rolling into decline; the new revenue lines must keep compounding toward management's 2028 target; free cash flow must stabilise near $210 million rather than continuing to fall; and the company must not spend its way through the balance sheet with further acquisitions at eight times revenue.
bear_thesis:
The bearish case is that Yelp is a toll booth on a road that is being rerouted, and that the cheapness is the market correctly discounting a business whose customer count, consumer traffic and cash flow are all falling at once.

Begin with the disclosure management gave away almost in passing. Ad clicks fell 3%, 7% and 11% through 2025 and another 10% in the first quarter of 2026, while the average price per click rose 9%, 11%, 14% and 8%. Asked about it, the chief financial officer explained: 'in terms of clicks lower and CPCs higher, that's going to be a natural outcome because we have the budget to deploy.' Read that carefully. Advertisers commit a budget; Yelp auctions a shrinking pool of consumer attention against it; prices rise because supply is falling. That is not pricing power, it is scarcity in the raw material. Confirming it, app unique devices fell 2% in 2025, and paying advertising locations fell 6% year over year to 485,000 in the first quarter of 2026. Both sides of the marketplace are contracting.

The structural cause is not a mystery. When a consumer asks a conversational assistant where to eat or who to hire, no Yelp page loads and no click is billed. Yelp's answer - license the data to the assistants - is rational but it is a trade down: it swaps a high-margin consumer destination that captures the full advertising dollar for a wholesale data contract with no disclosed economics, no disclosed term, and no exclusivity. When Bank of America asked in the first quarter of 2026 why Yelp content appears 'relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor' inside ChatGPT, the chief executive answered: 'we can't really comment on that nor do we have all the details of their plans.' Yelp cannot describe the placement or the economics of its most-promoted partnership. And every one of those licensing counterparties - OpenAI, Google, Apple, Amazon, Meta - has both the capital and the incentive to build or buy local content of its own once the category matters.

The peer group is the warning. Angi, the closest structural analogue, now trades at a $223 million market value, has negative earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation on a trailing basis, a negative 17% return on invested capital and negative free cash flow. Tripadvisor is at its own 52-week low with a 1.2% return on invested capital. This is what the end state of a disintermediated local-discovery platform looks like, and it does not arrive as a single bad quarter - it arrives as six years of macro excuses. Yelp has now blamed macro conditions for its restaurant and retail decline across four consecutive years while that decline accelerated from 3% to 11%.

The financial deterioration is already visible and is being masked. Quarterly net income fell from $44.1 million in the second quarter of 2025 to $31.7 million in the second quarter of 2026, down 28%; the first quarter fell 27%. Gross margin slipped from 90.4% to 88.9% as artificial-intelligence inference costs and lower-margin software revenue entered the cost line. Operating margin fell from 14.4% to 11.6%. Diluted earnings per share fell only from $0.67 to $0.57 - a smaller fall than net income - purely because the share count shrank. The buyback is doing the work the business is not.

And the buyback just slowed sharply. Repurchases ran $62.5 million, $65.9 million, $86.5 million, $88.7 million and then $124.0 million through the first quarter of 2026 - and then $50.0 million in the second quarter, a 60% cut in a single quarter, unremarked on the call. Meanwhile the balance sheet flipped: cash fell from $216 million at the end of 2025 to $94 million at 2026-06-30, the company drew $130 million of term debt in the first quarter, and now carries $100 million of borrowings and $23 million of capitalised leases against that cash - net debt of roughly $29 million where there was net cash six months ago. Yelp spent its cushion on Hatch ($264 million, about eight times that target's run-rate revenue, paid by a company whose own shares trade below one times revenue) and on its own stock. It is now paying interest into a rising-rate environment, with the ten-year Treasury above 5%.

The headline valuation is also flattered. The trailing free cash flow figure of $297 million that produces the sub-four-times multiple includes an unusually strong third quarter of 2025. First-half 2026 free cash flow was $106 million against $132 million in the first half of 2025, down 20%. On that run rate the business generates roughly $210 million, and the stock is on about ten and a half times the street's 2026 earnings estimate of $1.80 a share. Cheap, but not the three-and-a-half times the screen advertises - and ten times earnings for a business with no revenue growth, falling margins, falling returns and a shrinking customer base is not obviously wrong.

Finally, the people who know most are selling. Zero open-market purchases against 32 sales totalling 344,334 shares. The chief executive sold 20,479 shares at about $23.60 on 2026-08-20 and another executive sold 10,333 the same day. What would confirm the bear case: services advertising turning negative; the 2028 other-revenue target being softened or dropped; the buyback falling below $50 million a quarter or stopping; or a licensing partner in-sourcing local content.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is narrower than the screen suggests, and we want to be precise about it because the obvious disagreement is the wrong one.

The obvious disagreement - the one the screen prints - is that Yelp shows a huge margin of safety and trades at under four times free cash flow while seven brokers carry a Reduce consensus. We do not press that one, because the screen's cash flow figure is stale. The $297 million trailing free-cash-flow number is flattered by an unusually strong third quarter of 2025; first-half 2026 free cash flow was $106 million against $132 million a year earlier, down 20%. The honest forward run rate is roughly $210 million, which puts the enterprise near five times cash flow and the shares near ten and a half times the street's $1.80 estimate for 2026. Cheap, but not the extreme the screen advertises, and we will not build a position on a number we know to be backward-looking.

The disagreement we do press is compositional. The sell side and the tape are pricing Yelp as a single advertising business in terminal decline. It is two businesses with opposite trajectories plus a third that is growing fast. Restaurant and retail advertising, about $404 million a year, is genuinely melting at 11% and deserves the run-off multiple it is getting. Services advertising - plumbers, electricians, contractors, auto repair - is about $948 million, roughly two-thirds of advertising revenue, and it grew 1% rather than falling. It sells qualified leads for expensive, considered purchases, a materially harder job to disintermediate than a restaurant recommendation, and Yelp's own chatbot now originates 15% of quote requests versus about 5% a year ago. And other revenue - data licensing to Amazon Alexa, Apple Maps, Microsoft Bing, Meta.ai, Yahoo and OpenAI, plus Hatch software and DoorDash transactions - grew 75% to $29 million in the first quarter of 2026, with Hatch at a $34 million run rate growing 92% and Yelp Host past one million calls by June 2026. At today's enterprise value of roughly $1.09 billion the market is paying about one times a year's gross profit for all three of those things together. Our sum-of-the-parts says they are worth about $1.63 billion.

The specific street assumption we think is wrong is the one embedded in Morgan Stanley's standing Underweight and Bank of America's Underperform: that Yelp's relationship with conversational artificial intelligence is purely extractive. The evidence says otherwise - Yelp is a paid supplier to six of the largest platforms, and on 2026-09-10 became among the first companies anywhere to deploy OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 voice model commercially. That is not the behaviour of a company being routed around; it is a company selling the picks and shovels.

The assumption we think the bulls have wrong, and which stops us buying, is the mirror image: that the advertising franchise is merely cyclically depressed. The disclosure that kills that idea came from the chief financial officer himself on the 2025-11-06 call - 'in terms of clicks lower and CPCs higher, that's going to be a natural outcome because we have the budget to deploy.' Prices are rising because consumer attention is shrinking, not because advertisers value Yelp more. Paying locations are down 6%, app devices down 2%, clicks down 10%. That is an eroding franchise, and an eroding franchise is worth a discount even when it is cheap.

One more disagreement worth naming: the street's published view here barely exists. Not a single price target was issued in the last quarter, the newest is 130 days old, and no broker has changed a rating since 2026-05-15. When the consensus is eight stale targets averaging $30.63, it is not a view to arbitrage - it is an absence of a view, and the absence itself is the setup.
forcing_function:
There is no hard date that forces a re-rating here, and we will not pretend otherwise. What exists is a set of observable developments, each of which would change the argument, listed in the order we expect them.

The nearest dated item is the third-quarter 2026 earnings release, due roughly 44 days from our scan (early November 2026). It is an information release rather than an asymmetric event, but it carries the specific number that decides this case: whether services advertising revenue - about $948 million a year, roughly two-thirds of advertising - holds near flat or turns negative. Every other question is downstream of that one. We will also be reading paying advertising locations (485,000 in the first quarter of 2026, down 6% year over year) for any sign of stabilisation, and the quarterly repurchase figure.

The second is capital allocation. A re-acceleration of the buyback above $100 million a quarter, or a new repurchase authorisation announced alongside it, would tell us management believes its own valuation and would restore the per-share arithmetic. Continued restraint at $50 million a quarter, or a pause, would tell us the opposite - and given the balance sheet now carries net debt rather than net cash, restraint is the more likely path.

The third is the other-revenue trajectory against management's own target of a $250 million annual run rate by the end of 2028, set on the 2026-05-08 call. That target is the company's public commitment; progress reported each quarter against it is the cleanest scoreboard available, and it is the one number that could genuinely change the multiple by proving the business has a second engine. Disclosure of actual economics from the OpenAI relationship - term, exclusivity, or a dollar figure - would do the same in a single announcement.

The fourth is corporate action. Yelp has attracted activist attention in the past, and the current setup - a profitable company at 0.8 times a year's gross profit, with a founder-chief-executive, a melting segment that could be separated, and an abandoned sell side - is the textbook profile for an activist filing or a strategic review. We have found no current dated process and we do not underwrite one, but it is the single event that would close the gap to our $30 fastest.

Absent any of these, the honest answer is that this re-rates slowly, through several quarters of the advertising base proving it is flat rather than falling, or it does not re-rate at all.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next two to three quarters, and it has four distinct sources of pressure.

First, the earnings trend gets worse before it gets better. Quarterly net income has fallen 27% and then 28% year over year in the two reported quarters of 2026, and the street models full-year 2026 earnings of $1.80 a share against $2.24 delivered in 2025 - a 20% decline that has not yet fully printed. The third-quarter 2026 result, due in roughly 44 days (early November 2026), is the next test. The comparison is hard: the third quarter of 2025 delivered $376 million of revenue and $39 million of net income. If restaurant and retail advertising is still falling at double digits and services advertising fails to hold its 1% growth, the market will read that as the services half rolling over, which is precisely the event our adverse $16 case is built on.

Second, and most under-appreciated, the per-share arithmetic is weakening. Diluted earnings per share fell only from $0.67 to $0.57 while net income fell 28%, entirely because the share count shrank from 65.7 million to 55.7 million. That cushion is now thinner: buybacks ran $124.0 million in the first quarter of 2026 and then $50.0 million in the second, a 60% cut in one quarter that management did not address on the call. If the repurchase pace stays at $50 million while net income keeps falling, earnings per share falls with it and the one thing propping up the optics goes away.

Third, the balance sheet no longer provides a cushion. Cash fell from $216 million at the end of 2025 to $94 million at 2026-06-30 after the $264 million Hatch purchase and $174 million of first-half buybacks. The company drew $130 million of term debt in the first quarter and carries $100 million of borrowings plus $23 million of capitalised leases today - net debt of roughly $29 million where there was comfortable net cash six months ago. There is no maturity wall and no solvency question: this business still generates over $200 million a year and the Altman-Z solvency score of 2.1 is adequate. But the optionality is gone. Yelp cannot now fund another acquisition and an aggressive buyback at the same time.

Fourth, the macro backdrop is actively hostile to this profile. The Federal Reserve raised rates 25 basis points to 3.75-4.00% on 2026-09-16, sixteen of eighteen policymakers expect at least one further hike this year, and the ten-year Treasury closed above 5% for the first time since 2007. Rising discount rates compress the multiple on low-growth cash generators specifically, and Yelp is now paying interest ($1.6 million in the second quarter) into that environment. Separately, the same rate pressure squeezes the small local businesses that are Yelp's advertisers - management has flagged input costs and a weakened consumer for four straight years, and higher-for-longer rates do not relieve that.

What is not in the risky window: there is no cash-burn hump, no debt maturity wall, no covenant risk and no going-concern question. This is a profitable company. The risk is a grinding de-rating on deteriorating quarterly prints, not a crisis.
positioning_washout:
Forced-selling pressure here is largely spent, which is the single most constructive thing in the setup.

The shareholder base was never yield-focused - Yelp pays no dividend and never has - so there is no income fund facing a mechanical sale. What there was instead was a growth-and-quality shareholder base that has been steadily dismantled. The stock is at $19.195 against a 52-week high of $34.49, down 44%, trading 24% below its 200-day average and at the very bottom of its 52-week range. It printed a fresh 52-week low of $19.19 in today's session. Anyone who owned this as a growth name on the 2025 story has already been stopped out.

The sell side has effectively abandoned it. Seven brokers cover the name, the consensus recommendation was Reduce as of 2026-08-31 (two sell, four hold, one buy), no broker has changed a rating since 2026-05-15, and not a single price target has been published in the last quarter - the most recent is 130 days old. Coverage that stale is not a bearish view being expressed, it is coverage that has stopped being maintained. That matters mechanically: when nobody is publishing, nobody is downgrading, and the discretionary selling that follows downgrades has nowhere to come from.

The smart-money and institutional-flow readings in our scan are middling rather than distressed (33 and 52 out of 100), which argues the base is now mostly index and value holders rather than momentum money. The remaining mechanical risk is the market-capitalisation threshold: at roughly $1.06 billion Yelp sits near the boundary where small-capitalisation index membership starts to matter, and continued decline could eventually trigger index-driven selling. That is a real but second-order risk.

The offsetting negative, and it is not mechanical but it is loud, is insider behaviour. There have been zero open-market purchases against 32 sales totalling 344,334 shares. The chief executive sold 20,479 shares at about $23.60 on 2026-08-20 and a second executive sold 10,333 shares the same day. Insiders selling into their own 52-week low, with no offsetting purchase anywhere, is the clearest available read on internal conviction, and it argues that the people with the best information do not think the bottom is a bargain either.

Net: the forced sellers are gone, but no one - including management - is stepping up to buy, and the company itself has cut its own buying by 60%.
moderator_conclusion:
We are continuing coverage rather than starting fresh, and our conclusion is the same one we reached on 2026-09-04: this is a real value case wrapped around a real structural problem, and the right posture is to wait rather than to buy. We keep the wait-for-the-wash-out call and we keep the conviction score where it was. Nothing dated has changed in the business in the eighteen days since; what has changed is that the price fell another 11% to a fresh 52-week low of $19.19. A cheaper price on an unchanged thesis is not a reason to change the verdict, and the rule we hold ourselves to is that flips need new facts, not new feelings.

What we do owe the reader is precision about why we are not buying at a price this low, because the surface arithmetic is seductive. Yelp generates roughly 89% gross margins, has beaten its own guidance in all seven of the last seven quarters, has retired 10% of its shares in two quarters, and the whole enterprise is valued at about $1.09 billion against $1.30 billion of annual gross profit. Against a peer group where Tripadvisor earns a 1.2% return on invested capital and Angi's earnings are outright negative, Yelp is the only one actually making money.

Three things hold us back. First, the cheapness is partly an artefact. The headline free-cash-flow multiple rests on a trailing figure flattered by one strong quarter a year ago; first-half 2026 cash flow fell 20%, and on the honest run rate the stock is on roughly five times cash flow and ten and a half times this year's expected earnings. Genuinely cheap - but not the extreme the screen prints, and we size to the honest number.

Second, and decisively, the franchise is eroding while you would own it. Return on invested capital is about 9% and falling, return on equity 12.4% and falling, gross margin down from 90.4% to 88.9%, operating margin from 14.4% to 11.6%, paying advertiser locations down 6%, consumer devices down 2%, and clicks down 10% against prices up 8%. The chief financial officer explained that last pair himself in November 2025: prices rise because the company has 'the budget to deploy' against fewer clicks - which is scarcity in the raw material, not pricing power. High-but-falling returns on a shrinking customer base is an eroding moat, and our discipline is explicit that an eroding moat caps the value score at three regardless of how low the multiple goes. A cheap multiple on a structurally shrinking base is a trap, not a bargain. We apply that cap here.

Third, the safety net was spent. Six months ago Yelp had $216 million of cash and no debt; today it has $94 million of cash against $100 million of borrowings and $23 million of leases, having bought Hatch for $264 million at about eight times that target's revenue while its own shares trade below one times revenue. In the same window it cut its buyback 60% in a single quarter without mentioning it, and its chief executive sold 20,479 shares at about $23.60. Zero insiders bought. None of this is fatal - the company is solidly profitable and there is no maturity wall - but it removes the margin for error at exactly the moment the Federal Reserve raised rates to 3.75-4.00% and the ten-year Treasury closed above 5%.

Against all that, we want to be equally clear about what is genuinely good, because it is why this is a wait rather than a pass. The structural fear - that conversational artificial intelligence routes consumers around Yelp - is real and visible in the click data, but it is not the whole picture. Yelp now licenses its 330 million reviews to Amazon Alexa, Apple Maps, Microsoft Bing, Meta.ai, Yahoo and OpenAI, and on 2026-09-10 became among the first companies to commercially deploy OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 voice model inside Yelp Host and Hatch. That revenue line grew 75% year over year and management has staked a public target of a $250 million annual run rate by the end of 2028. Meanwhile the larger half of advertising - roughly $948 million of home and professional services leads - is flat, not falling, and is the hardest part of the business to disintermediate. Our sum-of-the-parts puts base-case fair value at $30 a share, with an adverse case at $16 and a favourable case at $40. We note, and disclose rather than bury, that $30 is $5.80 below the $35.80 we published two weeks ago - a tightening that comes from anchoring to peer multiples observed live today rather than from memory, since this whole cohort has de-rated.

On the catalyst, we apply our standing rule without flinching: this is a soft catalyst with no fixed date, and in this lane that is neither a plus nor a penalty. The dated-event names belong elsewhere in the book. We neither reward nor punish Yelp for the absence of a firm date; we judge the residual value case, and the residual value case is attractive on price and unattractive on durability.

So: what specifically are we waiting for? We will not hide behind a vague call to wait for a flush, so here are the named triggers. We would move to buying on any one of: first, the third-quarter 2026 result in early November showing services advertising revenue back to growth or paying advertising locations stabilising above 485,000 - the single number that separates our $30 case from our $16 case; second, the quarterly repurchase pace re-accelerating above $100 million or a fresh authorisation being announced, restoring the per-share arithmetic; third, disclosure of actual economics - a dollar figure, a term, or exclusivity - from the OpenAI relationship; or fourth, an activist filing or announced strategic review. Conversely, a print below $16 without any of the above would not be a buy signal but a confirmation of the adverse case, and we would step further back. And we would turn outright negative on services advertising revenue turning negative, or on the 2028 other-revenue target being softened or dropped.

In one line: Yelp is a genuinely profitable, genuinely cheap business that is genuinely getting worse, and at a 52-week low that combination earns our attention but not yet our capital.

interrogator_dossier:
# Yelp Inc. (YELP) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-09-22 · **Price used:** $19.195 (New York Stock Exchange, US dollars), the 52-week low
**Transcripts reviewed:** Q1 2025 (2025-05-08) · Q2 2025 (2025-08-08) · Q3 2025 (2025-11-06) · Q4/FY 2025 (2026-02-13) · Q1 2026 (2026-05-08)
**Coverage status:** continuing. This committee last wrote on 2026-09-04 at $21.66.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across five calls the story has been rebuilt from the ground up, and the rebuild is the single most important fact about this company.

**Spring 2025 — a two-speed advertising business.** The opening frame was simple and confident: one half of Yelp's advertising base (home and professional services — plumbers, contractors, auto repair) was compounding nicely, and the other half (restaurants, retail and what management calls "other") was suffering. Jeremy Stoppelman, the co-founder and chief executive, opened the first-quarter 2025 call with "Led by continued strength in our Services business, Yelp delivered 8% year-over-year revenue growth." Services advertising grew 14% that quarter — "the 16th consecutive quarter of double-digits year-over-year growth." Artificial intelligence appeared, but as a feature: better photo recognition inside the quote-request chatbot, smarter matching, summarised reviews.

**Summer 2025 — the first new revenue idea.** On the second-quarter 2025 call a genuinely new line entered the story: selling Yelp's review database to the companies building AI search products. "AI search API calls have accelerated, increasing by 20x over the past year and 10x in just the last 2 months," with annual run-rate revenue from AI search passing $10 million. Note what this is — Yelp reframing the technology that threatens it as a customer. That reframing has been the spine of every call since.

**Autumn 2025 — from advertising to software.** The third-quarter 2025 call introduced two subscription products: Yelp Host, a voice assistant that answers restaurant phones, and Yelp Receptionist, the equivalent for service businesses. This is the pivot in plain view — a company that had sold advertising clicks for twenty years began selling software seats.

**Winter 2026 — the pivot gets funded.** The fourth-quarter 2025 call (February 2026) announced the acquisition of Hatch, a lead-management software company for service professionals, and simultaneously retired Yelp Receptionist in its favour: "we've now shifted our focus in lead management from Yelp Receptionist to supporting the rapid growth of Hatch." A product announced in October was abandoned in February. That is fast, and it is honest, but it is also a tell about how little conviction the in-house build carried. Three strategic priorities were named for 2026: a conversational front end, software tools for businesses, and data licensing across the AI ecosystem. An agreement with OpenAI was disclosed.

**Spring 2026 — the advertising engine stalls, and the subject changes.** The first-quarter 2026 call is where the arc completes. Revenue grew 1%. Services advertising — the half that had grown double digits for sixteen straight quarters — grew 1%. Restaurants and retail fell 11%. And management's answer was a number about something else entirely: "other revenue grew 75% year-over-year," with a new target of "an annual run rate of $250 million in other revenue by the end of 2028, more than double the run rate delivered in the first quarter of this year."

**What was quietly dropped.** Three things. First, the "16 consecutive quarters of double-digit services growth" boast — it could not survive 2026 and has not been mentioned since. Second, the explicit stock-based-compensation glide path was still being repeated in Q1 2026 ("less than 6% of revenue by the end of 2027") but the more frequent, more granular capital-return commentary of 2025 has thinned. Third, and most tellingly, the specific quarterly disclosure of how much stock was repurchased and at what average price — a fixture of every 2025 call — has become less prominent exactly as the buyback was cut.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management's claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Services revenue increased by 14% year-over-year… 16th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth" (Q1 2025) | True then. The decay since is severe: +14% (Q1 2025) → +8% (Q2 2025) → +7% (Q3 2025) → **+1% (Q1 2026)**. | True, and now obsolete |
| "The main story behind the [restaurant] category is macro" (Q2 2025, Jed Nachman, chief operating officer) | Restaurant and retail advertising: −3% → −5% → −2% → −6% for full-year 2025 → **−11% in Q1 2026**. Four straight years of "macro" is not macro. | Deflection |
| "Record net revenue" (Q2 2025, Q3 2025, Q4 2025) | Technically true each time, but the growth behind it collapsed from 8% to 1%. Trailing-twelve-month revenue to 2026-06-30 is $1.47 billion, up roughly 1% on the prior year. | True but hollow |
| Strong profitability / "margin potential of our business" | Reversing. Quarterly net income: $44.1M (Q2 2025) → **$31.7M (Q2 2026), down 28%**. Diluted earnings per share $0.67 → $0.57. First-quarter 2026 net income fell 27%. Gross margin 90.4% → **88.9%**. | Diverging from the story |
| "Disciplined expense management" | Real but no longer sufficient. Operating expenses have been held roughly flat; the problem is that revenue stopped growing and cost of revenue is rising (AI inference and the lower-margin Hatch software business). | Partially true |
| Capital allocation: "returning excess capital to shareholders through share repurchases" | **This is the forensic finding of this review.** Repurchases by quarter: $62.5M (Q1 2025), $65.9M (Q2 2025), $86.5M (Q3 2025), $88.7M (Q4 2025), $124.0M (Q1 2026) — then **$50.0M in Q2 2026, a 60% cut in one quarter.** Nothing on the calls prepared shareholders for that. | Narrative and action diverge |
| Balance sheet strength / "maintaining a healthy cash balance" | Cash fell from $216M (2025-12-31) to **$94M (2026-06-30)**. The company drew $130M of term debt in Q1 2026 and carries $100M of borrowings plus $23M of capitalised leases today. **Net cash became net debt of roughly $29 million inside six months** — spent on Hatch ($264M) and on buying back stock. | Materially weaker than described |
| "Other revenue increased by 75% year-over-year to a record $29 million" (Q1 2026) | True, and the best thing in the file. But $29 million is 8% of quarterly revenue. Even on management's own 2028 target of $250M annual run-rate, this is roughly one-sixth of the company. | True, and too small to rescue the year |
| Hatch "annual run rate revenue exceeded $34 million in March, up 92% year-over-year" | Consistent with the price paid (about $264 million, roughly eight times run-rate revenue). Aggressive for a company whose own equity trades at less than one times revenue. | True, and expensive |

**The synthesis.** Every individual claim survives contact with the financial statements. What does not survive is the *impression* the claims leave in aggregate — that this is a profitable franchise compounding through a soft patch. The trailing-twelve-month free cash flow figure of $297 million that makes this stock look like it trades at under four times cash flow is backward-looking and flattered by an unusually strong third quarter of 2025. First-half 2026 free cash flow was **$106 million against $132 million in the first half of 2025, down 20%.** The honest forward run-rate is roughly $210-215 million, which puts the enterprise on about five times free cash flow — still cheap, but not the three-and-a-half times the headline suggests.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining, with one genuine exception.**

- *Q1 2025 — offensive.* "We remain excited by the opportunities ahead to drive profitable growth and shareholder value over the long-term." Guidance was raised at the revenue line.
- *Q2 2025 — first defensive note.* "We did not see the seasonal increase in revenue that we would typically expect." Management stopped promising seasonal recovery and started explaining its absence.
- *Q3 2025 — defensive, with a new offensive flank.* The advertising commentary is now purely about pressure; the energy has migrated entirely to new products. "Yelp's transformation with AI continues to accelerate."
- *Q4 2025 — reframing.* Chief financial officer David Schwarzbach opened not with the quarter but with a five-year retrospective on share-count reduction: "we reduced our fully diluted share count… from 86 million to 67 million, a 22% reduction." When a chief financial officer leads with five-year-old history, the current quarter is not the story he wants told.
- *Q1 2026 — the subject is fully changed.* Revenue growth of 1% is mentioned once. The transcript's energy is in Yelp Host, Hatch, and the OpenAI relationship.

**The exception is real.** On new products, management is specific in a way that evasive teams are not: call volumes, month-over-month growth rates, dated run-rate figures, a named 2028 target. Vague managements do not hand out numbers that can be checked later. This is confidence, not spin.

**The clearest non-answer in the file** came in Q1 2026, when Bank of America's Nitin Bansal asked directly why Yelp content appears "relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor" inside ChatGPT. Stoppelman's reply: "we can't really comment on that nor do we have all the details of their plans… continue to watch that space." The company cannot describe the economics or the placement of its single most-promoted partnership.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High. This is the strongest element of the entire file.**

Revenue has landed above the high end of the company's own outlook range in every quarter reviewed: $4M above (Q1 2025), $3M (Q2 2025), $6M (Q3 2025), $6M (Q1 2026), $8M (Q2 2026). Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation beat the high end by $15M, $11M, $13M and $15M respectively. The screener's independent count of seven beats in seven quarters corroborates the transcripts.

This is sandbagging, and it is systematic — the beats are too consistent and too one-directional to be forecasting noise. Two readings follow, and both matter. The benign one: this is a management team that will not over-promise, which is worth something when the operating environment is bad. The uncomfortable one: **guidance credibility is not the same as business quality.** A team can hit a low bar seven times while the bar itself descends. Yelp's full-year 2025 revenue guidance was widened in May, narrowed in August, and then *cut* in November ("we are lowering our outlook range for the full year… a decrease of $8 million at the midpoint"). They beat the quarter and lowered the year in the same breath.

**Reliability: High** on the quarter. **Medium** on the multi-year targets — the $250 million other-revenue run-rate by the end of 2028 is a 2026 promise about a 2028 outcome from a team that has already retired one product (Yelp Receptionist) four months after launching it.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**Recurring, and increasingly unanswered:**

1. **Why is the restaurant and retail base still shrinking after four years?** Asked every call, answered "macro" every call. The answer has not changed while the decline has accelerated to −11%.
2. **What are the actual economics of the AI partnerships?** Colin Sebastian of Baird asked in Q1 2026 whether these relationships generate "mostly referral traffic, off-platform monetization." He did not get a number. Management has disclosed a partner list (Amazon Alexa, Apple Maps, Microsoft Bing, Meta.ai, Yahoo, OpenAI) and an aggregate revenue line, but never per-partner economics, contract length, or exclusivity.
3. **Fewer clicks at higher prices — is that value creation or scarcity pricing?** Asked in Q1 2025, Q3 2025 and again in 2026. Ad clicks: −3%, −7%, −11%, −7% for full-year 2025, −10% in Q1 2026. Cost per click: +9%, +11%, +14%, +10%, +8%. Schwarzbach's Q3 2025 answer was candid — "in terms of clicks lower and CPCs higher, that's going to be a natural outcome because we have the budget to deploy" — which is an admission that rising prices reflect *falling supply of consumer attention*, not rising advertiser value. This is the most important disclosure in the file and analysts have not pressed hard enough on it.
4. **What analysts are not asking.** Nobody has publicly pushed on the buyback deceleration or on the balance sheet flipping from net cash to net debt. With zero price-target updates published in the last quarter and the most recent one 130 days old, there is barely a sell-side left to ask.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The buyback was cut 60% in one quarter without comment** — $124.0M in Q1 2026 to $50.0M in Q2 2026. The per-share arithmetic (diluted shares down from 62.0M to 55.7M in two quarters) is the main thing holding earnings per share up while net income falls. That engine just throttled back.

🔴 **Net cash became net debt inside six months.** $216M of cash at the end of 2025 is $94M today, against $100M of borrowings and $23M of leases. Yelp paid for Hatch and for its own stock out of the cushion. The company now has an interest expense line ($1.6M in Q2 2026) that did not exist a year ago — in a quarter when the Federal Reserve raised rates and the ten-year Treasury yield closed above 5% for the first time since 2007.

🔴 **Insider selling is one-directional.** Zero open-market purchases against 32 sales totalling 344,334 shares. The chief executive sold 20,479 shares at about $23.60 on 2026-08-20; a second executive sold 10,333 shares the same day. Insiders selling into a stock they publicly call undervalued, with no offsetting purchase, is the cleanest available read on internal conviction.

🔴 **Consumer engagement is falling, not just monetisation.** App unique devices were down 2% in 2025 "as consumers visited restaurants with reduced frequency," and paying advertising locations fell 6% year over year to 485,000 in Q1 2026. Both sides of the marketplace are contracting.

🔴 **A product was retired four months after launch.** Yelp Receptionist, announced October 2025, was shelved in February 2026 for an acquisition.

🟢 **Guidance delivery is genuinely excellent** — seven beats in seven quarters, every one above the high end of the company's own range.

🟢 **The new revenue lines are growing fast and are disclosed with checkable specifics.** Other revenue +75% year over year to $29 million in Q1 2026; Hatch at $34 million run-rate growing 92%; Yelp Host past one million calls by June 2026 at 38% average monthly growth since its October 2025 launch; food-ordering revenue +88%. Management notes these carry better margins than advertising: "when you look at licensing or transaction, that is almost entirely margin."

🟢 **Yelp is being paid by the technology that supposedly destroys it.** The OpenAI agreement (disclosed February 2026) and the integration of OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 voice model into Yelp Host and Hatch (announced 2026-09-10) place Yelp inside the AI stack as a supplier, not only as a casualty.

🟢 **Share count reduction is substantial and real** — fully diluted shares from 86 million (end 2021) to 67 million (end 2025), and the weighted diluted count is 55.7 million as of Q2 2026.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**"Advertising" has quietly stopped being the headline noun.** Compare the openings: Q1 2025 led with revenue growth "led by continued strength in our Services business"; Q1 2026 led with "Yelp continued to accelerate its AI transformation." The core business is now the thing mentioned after the strategy.

**"Other revenue" is doing enormous narrative work.** It is the only growth number management can say out loud, and it has been promoted from a footnote to the centre of the equity story in three quarters. Investors should notice that it is measured in run-rates and growth percentages, rarely in absolute dollars alongside the shrinking advertising base.

**The competitive frame changed from Google to OpenAI.** For a decade Google was the named adversary. Stoppelman still invoked that history in Q4 2025 — "for many years, we've competed with big tech players, particularly Google" — but only to argue that focus beats scale. The live question is now whether conversational assistants remove the need to visit Yelp at all, and management's answer is to sell them the data. That is a rational hedge and a real revenue line. It is also, structurally, the trade of a high-margin consumer destination for a lower-margin data supply contract.

**The voice on capital allocation shifted.** In 2025, Schwarzbach recited three priorities ending in "returning excess capital to shareholders through share repurchases." By Q1 2026 the ordering had become "investing in strategic transactions, driving traffic acquisition and returning excess capital." Buybacks moved from first-among-equals to last. The cash flow statement confirms the reordering was not rhetorical.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

This is not a stable business being mispriced, nor is it a collapsing one. It is a profitable advertising franchise whose core has stopped growing, being deliberately converted into a smaller, faster-growing software and data-licensing business — and the conversion is being paid for out of the balance-sheet cushion and, at the margin, out of the buyback that was holding per-share earnings together.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** the trailing free cash flow figure that makes this stock look like it trades at three-and-a-half times cash flow is not the forward figure. First-half 2026 free cash flow fell 20% year over year. On the honest run-rate, the enterprise trades near five times free cash flow and about nine to ten times this year's expected earnings — genuinely cheap, but not the extreme the headline screen implies. Size to the honest number, not the screen's.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and ERODING.** The moat type is an intangible brand supported by a content network — 330 million reviews and nearly 500 million photos that no competitor can recreate cheaply. That asset is real; it is precisely why OpenAI, Apple, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta pay for it. But the *evidence* in the financials points one way: return on invested capital of about 9% against a cost of capital that has risen with the rate environment; return on equity of 12.4% and falling; gross margin down from 90.4% to 88.9% year over year; operating margin from 14.4% to 11.6%; paying advertiser locations down 6%; consumer devices down 2%; ad clicks down 10% against prices up 8%. High-but-falling returns with an eroding gross margin and a shrinking customer count is an eroding moat by definition, not a wide one. The content asset retains value; the *advertising toll booth built on top of it* is losing pricing power over its supply of consumer attention.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The structural force is the displacement of navigational search by conversational AI assistants — a consumer who asks an assistant for a plumber may never load a Yelp page, and Yelp's advertising revenue is charged per click on a Yelp page. That risk is live and it is visibly in the click data. Three things stop it short of terminal. First, the home-and-professional-services half of the advertising base — roughly $948 million a year, about two-thirds of advertising revenue — sells qualified leads for high-consideration purchases, which is a harder job to disintermediate than a restaurant recommendation, and it is flat rather than falling. Second, Yelp is a paid supplier to the displacing technology, not only its victim. Third, the software products (Hatch, Yelp Host) are sold to local businesses as tools, not as ad inventory, and are growing 75-92%.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Honestly, it is both, in measurable proportion. The restaurant and retail advertising line — roughly $404 million a year falling at 11% — is a genuine melting asset and deserves a run-off multiple. The services advertising line plus the new revenue legs are not melting, and at today's price the market is paying close to nothing for them. The correct posture is neither the 180% margin of safety the screen prints nor the "Reduce" the sell side prints, but a disciplined mid-point with the position sized for the fact that the franchise is eroding while you own it.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory turning · a moat that is being eroded · moat trend eroding · structural threat material.

bull_thesis:
The bullish case is that the market has confused a shrinking part of Yelp with the whole of it, and is now paying almost nothing for the parts that are not shrinking.

Start with what you are buying at $19.195 a share. With about 55.0 million shares outstanding the equity is worth roughly $1.06 billion, and after netting $94 million of cash against $100 million of borrowings and $23 million of capitalised leases the whole enterprise is valued at about $1.09 billion. Against that, the trailing twelve months to 2026-06-30 produced $1.47 billion of revenue, $1.30 billion of gross profit (an 88.5% gross margin), $184 million of operating profit, $126 million of net income and $297 million of free cash flow. The enterprise therefore trades at roughly 0.8 times a year's gross profit and under six times operating profit. For a business with no inventory, no factories and negligible capital spending, those are the multiples of a company expected to disappear.

It is not disappearing, and the segment detail shows why. Yelp's advertising revenue splits into two very different businesses. The larger one, advertising to home and professional services - plumbers, electricians, contractors, auto repair - runs at about $948 million a year and grew 1% in the first quarter of 2026. It is flat, not falling. It sells qualified leads for expensive, high-consideration purchases, which is a much harder job for a chatbot to take away than a dinner recommendation, and Yelp is actively improving it: its chatbot, Yelp Assistant, now originates 15% of all quote requests, up from about 5% a year earlier, and management has said that excluding projects bought through paid search, quote-request volume grew roughly 15% in 2025. The smaller advertising business - restaurants, retail and other - runs at about $404 million and fell 11% in the first quarter of 2026. That one is genuinely melting. The bull case does not deny it; it says you are already being compensated for it several times over.

Then there is the part nobody is paying for. Other revenue reached $29 million in the first quarter of 2026, up 75% year over year, and roughly $32 million in the second quarter. It has three legs, all growing fast and all higher-margin than advertising. Data licensing: Yelp has signed Amazon Alexa, Apple Maps, Microsoft Bing, Meta.ai, Yahoo and, in February 2026, OpenAI, to license its 330 million reviews, 500 million photos and 8 million business listings - the exact asset every conversational assistant needs and cannot cheaply build. Software: Hatch, acquired in February 2026, was at a $34 million annual run rate in March growing 92%; Yelp Host passed one million calls answered by June 2026, having grown at an average 38% a month since its October 2025 launch, and management sizes its United States market at over $1 billion. Transactions: food ordering revenue grew 88% year over year on the DoorDash partnership. Management targets a $250 million annual run rate for this combined line by the end of 2028, more than double the current pace. On 2026-09-10 Yelp and Hatch became among the first deployers of OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 voice model - the company that is supposed to kill Yelp is instead its supplier and its customer.

The quality of the business supports the case. Gross margin is 88.9%. Return on invested capital is about 9% and return on equity 12.4% - modest in absolute terms, but set against Tripadvisor's 1.2% return on invested capital and Angi's negative 17%, Yelp is the only member of its peer group actually earning money. Management has beaten the top end of its own revenue guidance in all seven of the last seven quarters, and beaten its adjusted profit guidance by $11 million to $15 million a quarter. And the share count has fallen hard: fully diluted shares went from 86 million at the end of 2021 to 67 million at the end of 2025, and the weighted diluted count was 55.7 million in the second quarter of 2026 - down another 10% in just two quarters. Every dollar of flat earnings is spread across a steadily smaller base.

Finally, positioning. Seven brokers cover the stock, the consensus recommendation was Reduce as of 2026-08-31, there has been no rating change by anyone since 2026-05-15, and not a single price target was published in the last quarter - the most recent is 130 days old. The stock is at its 52-week low, 24% below its 200-day average. There is essentially nobody left to sell it on the next disappointment.

Conditions this case depends on: services advertising must hold near flat rather than rolling into decline; the new revenue lines must keep compounding toward management's 2028 target; free cash flow must stabilise near $210 million rather than continuing to fall; and the company must not spend its way through the balance sheet with further acquisitions at eight times revenue.
bear_thesis:
The bearish case is that Yelp is a toll booth on a road that is being rerouted, and that the cheapness is the market correctly discounting a business whose customer count, consumer traffic and cash flow are all falling at once.

Begin with the disclosure management gave away almost in passing. Ad clicks fell 3%, 7% and 11% through 2025 and another 10% in the first quarter of 2026, while the average price per click rose 9%, 11%, 14% and 8%. Asked about it, the chief financial officer explained: 'in terms of clicks lower and CPCs higher, that's going to be a natural outcome because we have the budget to deploy.' Read that carefully. Advertisers commit a budget; Yelp auctions a shrinking pool of consumer attention against it; prices rise because supply is falling. That is not pricing power, it is scarcity in the raw material. Confirming it, app unique devices fell 2% in 2025, and paying advertising locations fell 6% year over year to 485,000 in the first quarter of 2026. Both sides of the marketplace are contracting.

The structural cause is not a mystery. When a consumer asks a conversational assistant where to eat or who to hire, no Yelp page loads and no click is billed. Yelp's answer - license the data to the assistants - is rational but it is a trade down: it swaps a high-margin consumer destination that captures the full advertising dollar for a wholesale data contract with no disclosed economics, no disclosed term, and no exclusivity. When Bank of America asked in the first quarter of 2026 why Yelp content appears 'relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor' inside ChatGPT, the chief executive answered: 'we can't really comment on that nor do we have all the details of their plans.' Yelp cannot describe the placement or the economics of its most-promoted partnership. And every one of those licensing counterparties - OpenAI, Google, Apple, Amazon, Meta - has both the capital and the incentive to build or buy local content of its own once the category matters.

The peer group is the warning. Angi, the closest structural analogue, now trades at a $223 million market value, has negative earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation on a trailing basis, a negative 17% return on invested capital and negative free cash flow. Tripadvisor is at its own 52-week low with a 1.2% return on invested capital. This is what the end state of a disintermediated local-discovery platform looks like, and it does not arrive as a single bad quarter - it arrives as six years of macro excuses. Yelp has now blamed macro conditions for its restaurant and retail decline across four consecutive years while that decline accelerated from 3% to 11%.

The financial deterioration is already visible and is being masked. Quarterly net income fell from $44.1 million in the second quarter of 2025 to $31.7 million in the second quarter of 2026, down 28%; the first quarter fell 27%. Gross margin slipped from 90.4% to 88.9% as artificial-intelligence inference costs and lower-margin software revenue entered the cost line. Operating margin fell from 14.4% to 11.6%. Diluted earnings per share fell only from $0.67 to $0.57 - a smaller fall than net income - purely because the share count shrank. The buyback is doing the work the business is not.

And the buyback just slowed sharply. Repurchases ran $62.5 million, $65.9 million, $86.5 million, $88.7 million and then $124.0 million through the first quarter of 2026 - and then $50.0 million in the second quarter, a 60% cut in a single quarter, unremarked on the call. Meanwhile the balance sheet flipped: cash fell from $216 million at the end of 2025 to $94 million at 2026-06-30, the company drew $130 million of term debt in the first quarter, and now carries $100 million of borrowings and $23 million of capitalised leases against that cash - net debt of roughly $29 million where there was net cash six months ago. Yelp spent its cushion on Hatch ($264 million, about eight times that target's run-rate revenue, paid by a company whose own shares trade below one times revenue) and on its own stock. It is now paying interest into a rising-rate environment, with the ten-year Treasury above 5%.

The headline valuation is also flattered. The trailing free cash flow figure of $297 million that produces the sub-four-times multiple includes an unusually strong third quarter of 2025. First-half 2026 free cash flow was $106 million against $132 million in the first half of 2025, down 20%. On that run rate the business generates roughly $210 million, and the stock is on about ten and a half times the street's 2026 earnings estimate of $1.80 a share. Cheap, but not the three-and-a-half times the screen advertises - and ten times earnings for a business with no revenue growth, falling margins, falling returns and a shrinking customer base is not obviously wrong.

Finally, the people who know most are selling. Zero open-market purchases against 32 sales totalling 344,334 shares. The chief executive sold 20,479 shares at about $23.60 on 2026-08-20 and another executive sold 10,333 the same day. What would confirm the bear case: services advertising turning negative; the 2028 other-revenue target being softened or dropped; the buyback falling below $50 million a quarter or stopping; or a licensing partner in-sourcing local content.

Where we disagree with the market is narrower than the screen suggests, and we want to be precise about it because the obvious disagreement is the wrong one.

The obvious disagreement - the one the screen prints - is that Yelp shows a huge margin of safety and trades at under four times free cash flow while seven brokers carry a Reduce consensus. We do not press that one, because the screen's cash flow figure is stale. The $297 million trailing free-cash-flow number is flattered by an unusually strong third quarter of 2025; first-half 2026 free cash flow was $106 million against $132 million a year earlier, down 20%. The honest forward run rate is roughly $210 million, which puts the enterprise near five times cash flow and the shares near ten and a half times the street's $1.80 estimate for 2026. Cheap, but not the extreme the screen advertises, and we will not build a position on a number we know to be backward-looking.

The disagreement we do press is compositional. The sell side and the tape are pricing Yelp as a single advertising business in terminal decline. It is two businesses with opposite trajectories plus a third that is growing fast. Restaurant and retail advertising, about $404 million a year, is genuinely melting at 11% and deserves the run-off multiple it is getting. Services advertising - plumbers, electricians, contractors, auto repair - is about $948 million, roughly two-thirds of advertising revenue, and it grew 1% rather than falling. It sells qualified leads for expensive, considered purchases, a materially harder job to disintermediate than a restaurant recommendation, and Yelp's own chatbot now originates 15% of quote requests versus about 5% a year ago. And other revenue - data licensing to Amazon Alexa, Apple Maps, Microsoft Bing, Meta.ai, Yahoo and OpenAI, plus Hatch software and DoorDash transactions - grew 75% to $29 million in the first quarter of 2026, with Hatch at a $34 million run rate growing 92% and Yelp Host past one million calls by June 2026. At today's enterprise value of roughly $1.09 billion the market is paying about one times a year's gross profit for all three of those things together. Our sum-of-the-parts says they are worth about $1.63 billion.

The specific street assumption we think is wrong is the one embedded in Morgan Stanley's standing Underweight and Bank of America's Underperform: that Yelp's relationship with conversational artificial intelligence is purely extractive. The evidence says otherwise - Yelp is a paid supplier to six of the largest platforms, and on 2026-09-10 became among the first companies anywhere to deploy OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 voice model commercially. That is not the behaviour of a company being routed around; it is a company selling the picks and shovels.

The assumption we think the bulls have wrong, and which stops us buying, is the mirror image: that the advertising franchise is merely cyclically depressed. The disclosure that kills that idea came from the chief financial officer himself on the 2025-11-06 call - 'in terms of clicks lower and CPCs higher, that's going to be a natural outcome because we have the budget to deploy.' Prices are rising because consumer attention is shrinking, not because advertisers value Yelp more. Paying locations are down 6%, app devices down 2%, clicks down 10%. That is an eroding franchise, and an eroding franchise is worth a discount even when it is cheap.

One more disagreement worth naming: the street's published view here barely exists. Not a single price target was issued in the last quarter, the newest is 130 days old, and no broker has changed a rating since 2026-05-15. When the consensus is eight stale targets averaging $30.63, it is not a view to arbitrage - it is an absence of a view, and the absence itself is the setup.
forcing_function:
There is no hard date that forces a re-rating here, and we will not pretend otherwise. What exists is a set of observable developments, each of which would change the argument, listed in the order we expect them.

The nearest dated item is the third-quarter 2026 earnings release, now roughly 35 days out from this 2026-09-29 update (early November 2026). It is an information release rather than an asymmetric event, but it carries the specific number that decides this case: whether services advertising revenue - about $948 million a year, roughly two-thirds of advertising - holds near flat or turns negative. Every other question is downstream of that one. We will also be reading paying advertising locations (485,000 in the first quarter of 2026, down 6% year over year) for any sign of stabilisation, and the quarterly repurchase figure.

The second is capital allocation. A re-acceleration of the buyback above $100 million a quarter, or a new repurchase authorisation announced alongside it, would tell us management believes its own valuation and would restore the per-share arithmetic. Continued restraint at $50 million a quarter, or a pause, would tell us the opposite - and given the balance sheet now carries net debt rather than net cash, restraint is the more likely path.

The third is the other-revenue trajectory against management's own target of a $250 million annual run rate by the end of 2028, set on the 2026-05-08 call. That target is the company's public commitment; progress reported each quarter against it is the cleanest scoreboard available, and it is the one number that could genuinely change the multiple by proving the business has a second engine. Disclosure of actual economics from the OpenAI relationship - term, exclusivity, or a dollar figure - would do the same in a single announcement.

The fourth is corporate action. Yelp has attracted activist attention in the past, and the current setup - a profitable company at roughly one times a year's gross profit, with a founder-chief-executive, a melting segment that could be separated, and an abandoned sell side - is the textbook profile for an activist filing or a strategic review. As of this 2026-09-29 update a 24/7 Wall Street piece has named Yelp as its top take-private pick on this same logic, but explicitly confirms no takeover report or activist filing has actually appeared. We have found no current dated process and we do not underwrite one, but it is the single event that would close the gap to our $30 fastest.

Absent any of these, the honest answer is that this re-rates slowly, through several quarters of the advertising base proving it is flat rather than falling, or it does not re-rate at all.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next two to three quarters, and it has four distinct sources of pressure.

First, the earnings trend gets worse before it gets better. Quarterly net income has fallen 27% and then 28% year over year in the two reported quarters of 2026, and the street models full-year 2026 earnings of $1.80 a share against $2.24 delivered in 2025 - a 20% decline that has not yet fully printed. The third-quarter 2026 result, now roughly 35 days out from this update (early November 2026), is the next test. The comparison is hard: the third quarter of 2025 delivered $376 million of revenue and $39 million of net income. If restaurant and retail advertising is still falling at double digits and services advertising fails to hold its 1% growth, the market will read that as the services half rolling over, which is precisely the event our adverse $16 case is built on.

Second, and most under-appreciated, the per-share arithmetic is weakening. Diluted earnings per share fell only from $0.67 to $0.57 while net income fell 28%, entirely because the share count shrank from 65.7 million to 55.7 million. That cushion is now thinner: buybacks ran $124.0 million in the first quarter of 2026 and then $50.0 million in the second, a 60% cut in one quarter that management did not address on the call. If the repurchase pace stays at $50 million while net income keeps falling, earnings per share falls with it and the one thing propping up the optics goes away.

Third, the balance sheet no longer provides a cushion. Cash fell from $216 million at the end of 2025 to $94 million at 2026-06-30 after the $264 million Hatch purchase and $174 million of first-half buybacks. The company drew $130 million of term debt in the first quarter and carries $100 million of borrowings plus $23 million of capitalised leases today - net debt of roughly $29 million where there was comfortable net cash six months ago. There is no maturity wall and no solvency question: this business still generates over $200 million a year and the Altman-Z solvency score of 2.1 is adequate. But the optionality is gone. Yelp cannot now fund another acquisition and an aggressive buyback at the same time.

Fourth, the macro backdrop is actively hostile to this profile. The Federal Reserve raised rates 25 basis points to 3.75-4.00% on 2026-09-16, sixteen of eighteen policymakers expect at least one further hike this year, and the ten-year Treasury closed above 5% for the first time since 2007. Rising discount rates compress the multiple on low-growth cash generators specifically, and Yelp is now paying interest ($1.6 million in the second quarter) into that environment. Separately, the same rate pressure squeezes the small local businesses that are Yelp's advertisers - management has flagged input costs and a weakened consumer for four straight years, and higher-for-longer rates do not relieve that.

What is not in the risky window: there is no cash-burn hump, no debt maturity wall, no covenant risk and no going-concern question. This is a profitable company. The risk is a grinding de-rating on deteriorating quarterly prints, not a crisis.
positioning_washout:
Forced-selling pressure here is largely spent, which is the single most constructive thing in the setup.

The shareholder base was never yield-focused - Yelp pays no dividend and never has - so there is no income fund facing a mechanical sale. What there was instead was a growth-and-quality shareholder base that has been steadily dismantled. The stock is at $19.195 against a 52-week high of $34.49, down 44%, trading 24% below its 200-day average and at the very bottom of its 52-week range. It printed a fresh 52-week low of $19.19 in today's session. Anyone who owned this as a growth name on the 2025 story has already been stopped out. As of this 2026-09-29 update the shares have fallen a further 7.9% to $17.675 with a new intraday low of $17.64 recorded 2026-09-24; we found no new deterioration in sell-side coverage or smart-money/institutional-flow readings since the anchor, so this reads as the same washout continuing rather than a new one starting.

The sell side has effectively abandoned it. Seven brokers cover the name, the consensus recommendation was Reduce as of 2026-08-31 (two sell, four hold, one buy), no broker has changed a rating since 2026-05-15, and not a single price target has been published in the last quarter - the most recent is 130 days old. Coverage that stale is not a bearish view being expressed, it is coverage that has stopped being maintained. That matters mechanically: when nobody is publishing, nobody is downgrading, and the discretionary selling that follows downgrades has nowhere to come from.

The smart-money and institutional-flow readings in our scan are middling rather than distressed (33 and 52 out of 100), which argues the base is now mostly index and value holders rather than momentum money. The remaining mechanical risk is the market-capitalisation threshold: at roughly $971 million as of this update Yelp sits at the boundary where small-capitalisation index membership starts to matter, and continued decline could eventually trigger index-driven selling. That is a real but second-order risk, and it has moved closer with the price decline.

The offsetting negative, and it is not mechanical but it is loud, is insider behaviour. There have been zero open-market purchases against 32 sales totalling 344,334 shares, unchanged since the anchor (no new Form 4 sales filed through 2026-09-29). The chief executive sold 20,479 shares at about $23.60 on 2026-08-20 and a second executive sold 10,333 shares the same day. Insiders selling into a price now 25% above today's quote, with no offsetting purchase anywhere, is the clearest available read on internal conviction, and it argues that the people with the best information do not think the bottom is a bargain either.

Net: the forced sellers are gone, but no one - including management - is stepping up to buy, and the company itself has cut its own buying by 60%.
moderator_conclusion:
We are continuing coverage rather than starting fresh, and our conclusion is the same one we reached on 2026-09-04 and reaffirmed on 2026-09-22: this is a real value case wrapped around a real structural problem, and the right posture is to wait rather than to buy. We keep the wait-for-the-wash-out call and we keep the conviction score where it was. Nothing dated has changed in the business since our 2026-09-22 anchor; what has changed is that the price fell another 7.9% to $17.675, printing a fresh 52-week low along the way, with no new company-specific fact behind the move and no new insider selling. A cheaper price on an unchanged thesis is not a reason to change the verdict, and the rule we hold ourselves to is that flips need new facts, not new feelings.

What we do owe the reader is precision about why we are not buying at a price this low, because the surface arithmetic is seductive. Yelp generates roughly 89% gross margins, has beaten its own guidance in all seven of the last seven quarters, has retired 10% of its shares in two quarters, and the whole enterprise is valued at roughly $1.0 billion against $1.30 billion of annual gross profit. Against a peer group where Tripadvisor earns a 1.2% return on invested capital and Angi's earnings are outright negative, Yelp is the only one actually making money.

Three things hold us back, unchanged from the anchor. First, the cheapness is partly an artefact. The headline free-cash-flow multiple rests on a trailing figure flattered by one strong quarter a year ago; first-half 2026 cash flow fell 20%, and on the honest run rate the stock is on a mid-single-digit multiple of cash flow and roughly ten times this year's expected earnings. Genuinely cheap - but not the extreme the screen prints, and we size to the honest number.

Second, and decisively, the franchise is eroding while you would own it. Return on invested capital is about 9% and falling, return on equity 12.4% and falling, gross margin down from 90.4% to 88.9%, operating margin from 14.4% to 11.6%, paying advertiser locations down 6%, consumer devices down 2%, and clicks down 10% against prices up 8%. The chief financial officer explained that last pair himself in November 2025: prices rise because the company has 'the budget to deploy' against fewer clicks - which is scarcity in the raw material, not pricing power. High-but-falling returns on a shrinking customer base is an eroding moat, and our discipline is explicit that an eroding moat caps the value score at three regardless of how low the multiple goes. A cheap multiple on a structurally shrinking base is a trap, not a bargain. We apply that cap here.

Third, the safety net was spent. A year ago Yelp had $216 million of cash and no debt; today it has $94 million of cash against $100 million of borrowings and $23 million of leases, having bought Hatch for $264 million at about eight times that target's revenue while its own shares trade below one times revenue. In the same window it cut its buyback 60% in a single quarter without mentioning it, and its chief executive sold 20,479 shares at about $23.60. Zero insiders have bought since, through this update. None of this is fatal - the company is solidly profitable and there is no maturity wall - but it removes the margin for error at exactly the moment the Federal Reserve raised rates to 3.75-4.00% and the ten-year Treasury closed above 5%.

Against all that, we want to be equally clear about what is genuinely good, because it is why this is a wait rather than a pass. The structural fear - that conversational artificial intelligence routes consumers around Yelp - is real and visible in the click data, but it is not the whole picture. Yelp now licenses its 330 million reviews to Amazon Alexa, Apple Maps, Microsoft Bing, Meta.ai, Yahoo and OpenAI, and on 2026-09-10 became among the first companies to commercially deploy OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 voice model inside Yelp Host and Hatch. That revenue line grew 75% year over year and management has staked a public target of a $250 million annual run rate by the end of 2028. Meanwhile the larger half of advertising - roughly $948 million of home and professional services leads - is flat, not falling, and is the hardest part of the business to disintermediate. Our sum-of-the-parts puts base-case fair value at $30 a share, with an adverse case at $16 and a favourable case at $40 - all unchanged from the anchor, since no dated fact has moved them.

On the catalyst, we apply our standing rule without flinching: this is a soft catalyst with no fixed date, and in this lane that is neither a plus nor a penalty. We neither reward nor punish Yelp for the absence of a firm date; we judge the residual value case, and the residual value case is attractive on price and unattractive on durability - modestly more attractive on price than at the anchor, purely mechanically.

So: what specifically are we waiting for? Unchanged from the anchor: first, the third-quarter 2026 result in early November showing services advertising revenue back to growth or paying advertising locations stabilising above 485,000 - the single number that separates our $30 case from our $16 case; second, the quarterly repurchase pace re-accelerating above $100 million or a fresh authorisation being announced; third, disclosure of actual economics from the OpenAI relationship; or fourth, an activist filing or announced strategic review - on which a 2026-09-29 media piece raised the profile of the idea without any actual filing behind it. Conversely, a print below $16 without any of the above would not be a buy signal but a confirmation of the adverse case, and we would step further back. And we would turn outright negative on services advertising revenue turning negative, or on the 2028 other-revenue target being softened or dropped.

In one line: Yelp is a genuinely profitable, genuinely cheap business that is genuinely getting worse, and a further slide to a new 52-week low earns our continued attention but not yet our capital.
